title: Vishnu Sahasranamam Lyrics with Meaning: Verses 61-62
desc: Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 61 to 62 in Sanskrit with a simple English meaning and how to chant them: 'सुधन्वा खण्डपरशुर्दारुणो द्रविणप्रदः'.
alt: Lord Vishnu, Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 61 to 62 with meaning
caption: Vishnu Sahasranamam, verses 61 to 62.
intro: **Vishnu Sahasranamam** is the thousand names of Lord Vishnu, taught by Bhishma to Yudhishthira in the Mahabharata. This post gives **verses 61 to 62** with the Sanskrit text and a plain English meaning, so you can chant with understanding.
takeaways: The verses here open with **सुधन्वा खण्डपरशुर्दारुणो द्रविणप्रदः**.
Read the Sanskrit slowly, then the meaning, then chant once more.
Thursday and Ekadashi are the days most families keep for Vishnu Sahasranamam.
A short daily portion is better than a rushed full reading.

p: Read the lines aloud, one breath for each half of a verse:
**सुधन्वा खण्डपरशुर्दारुणो द्रविणप्रदः । दिवःस्पृक्सर्वदृग्व्यासो वाचस्पतिरयोनिजः ॥** **त्रिसामा सामगः साम निर्वाणं भेषजं भिषक् । संन्यासकृच्छमः शान्तो निष्ठा शान्तिः परायणम् ॥**

He bears the fine bow and the axe, stern, and a giver of wealth. The one who touches the sky, sees all and is Vyasa, is that God of gods. Lord of speech, born of no womb. He has the three Samas and sings the Sama. The Sama itself, liberation, the medicine and the physician is that God of gods. He grants renunciation and calm; peaceful, the firm ground, peace itself and the final refuge.
Light a lamp, sit facing east and chant these verses once, then read the meaning silently. Many families take two verses a day and finish the full text in a little under two months.
The names do not need a long ritual. What matters is steady practice, a clear pronunciation and a calm mind.

ul: Thursdays, the day of Vishnu and the planet Jupiter.
Early morning after a bath, or in the evening at the lamp.

faq.q: What do Vishnu Sahasranamam verses 61 to 62 mean?
faq.a: He bears the fine bow and the axe, stern, and a giver of wealth. The one who touches the sky, sees all and is Vyasa, is that God of gods. Lord of speech, born of no womb. He has the three Samas and sings the Sama. The Sama itself, liberation, the medicine and the physician is that God of gods. He grants renunciation and calm; peaceful, the firm ground, peace itself and the final refuge.
**Bhishma** taught it to Yudhishthira on the field of Kurukshetra, as told in the Anushasana Parva of the Mahabharata.

faq.q: Can I chant a few verses a day instead of the whole text?
faq.a: Yes. A small daily portion with the meaning understood is a common and accepted way to learn it.

note: The Sanskrit is the traditional text. The English is our own plain rendering of the meaning.
